prompts.text: What makes it easier to understand someone whose communication style differs from yours?
Tell me about discovering that a person you misunderstood was trying to be considerate.
Two colleagues interpret the same short message differently. What context would help them understand it?
Ask for clarification immediately or explain how you interpreted a message first?
People often rely on tone and timing as much as the words in a conversation.
Asking what someone meant is more useful than building a theory about their intentions.
When do you prefer a direct answer over a gentler explanation?
Recall a conversation when a small clarification prevented a much larger misunderstanding.
Someone takes your quietness as disagreement. How would you explain what silence means for you?
Discuss an important issue by phone or in person where you can read each other's reactions?
Which quality do you notice first in somebody who makes others feel included?
Describe a time a group welcomed you without asking you to change your personality.
A new person joins a close group but struggles with existing inside jokes. What would you want the others to notice?
Include someone by asking their opinion or by inviting them into a shared activity?
Belonging sometimes begins with being remembered rather than being the centre of attention.
A group isn't particularly welcoming if everyone has to behave in the same way to fit in.
How do you recognise when someone feels left out even though they're smiling?
Tell me about a person who helped you feel part of something unfamiliar.
One participant rarely speaks during a lively discussion. How would you find out whether they want a turn?
A gathering with structured introductions or one where people connect in smaller conversations?
How have your expectations of friendship changed since your teenage years?
Tell me about becoming closer to someone after a difficult but respectful disagreement.
Two old friends now lead very different lives. What could help them maintain a connection without forcing old routines?
A friendship built on frequent conversations or on shared experiences over many years?
The reasons people become friends sometimes differ from the reasons they stay friends.
Friendships deserve the freedom to change without automatically being considered weaker.
What kind of change in a friend would make you curious rather than concerned?
Recall realising a casual acquaintance had become someone you relied on.
A friend develops a new interest that changes their social schedule. How might the friendship adapt?
Reconnect through a shared childhood memory or discover something new about each other's present lives?
What helps you decide which details about your life you're comfortable sharing?
Describe a time someone respected your privacy without asking for an explanation.
A relative asks about a personal decision during a public gathering. What would help you respond comfortably?
Set a boundary with a brief explanation or agree to discuss it privately later?
Different people distinguish privacy from secrecy in different ways.
Closeness doesn't entitle someone to every detail of another person's life.
How can a person show interest in you without asking questions that feel intrusive?
Tell me about learning an important boundary by listening rather than making assumptions.
A friend shares news with you but not the rest of the group. How do you handle later questions?
Ask whether a subject is comfortable before discussing it or let the person introduce it themselves?
Which small action tells you somebody is dependable?
Recall someone fulfilling a promise you had almost forgotten they'd made.
Two friends agree to help organise an event, but one becomes unexpectedly busy. What would responsible follow-up look like?
A person who gives realistic commitments or one who volunteers enthusiastically and adjusts later?
Reliability becomes visible through ordinary decisions long before a crisis arrives.
Clear limits often build more trust than ambitious promises.
What would make you reconsider an early negative impression of someone's reliability?
Describe discovering that somebody had quietly prepared for something important to you.
A person misses an agreed deadline but tells you promptly and offers a solution. What matters most in your response?
Receive a timely update about a delay or an unexpected effort to make up for it?
What makes it easier to talk about disappointment without blaming somebody?
Tell me about discussing a disagreement with someone who helped you feel understood.
Two people remember an agreement differently. What should happen before either assigns blame?
Begin with how an event affected you or with your understanding of what happened?
People sometimes need time to distinguish disappointment from anger.
A fair disagreement includes room for somebody to change their mind.
What usually tells you that a difficult conversation is becoming productive?
Recall an apology that made a difference because the person's behaviour changed afterwards.
Someone wants to make amends but isn't sure what the other person needs. What could they ask?
Repair a misunderstanding through conversation or through an agreed practical change?
Which relationship in your life taught you the most about patience?
Describe learning something unexpected from a person whose pace was different from yours.
A younger family member is eager to make a decision an older relative considers premature. What might each learn by listening?
Learn from a mentor with a different background or from a peer facing similar experiences?
Differences in life stage can shape the same relationship in very different ways.
Respect across generations requires curiosity in both directions.
How do you recognise advice that comes from experience rather than from personal preference?
Tell me about a conversation with an elder that changed your understanding of their choices.
Two relatives disagree about what counts as an important milestone. How would you explore their reasons?
Ask someone about a decision they regret or a decision they're still glad they made?
How do you tell when somebody wants solutions rather than understanding?
Describe a time practical help mattered more to you than encouraging words.
A friend has a stressful week and doesn't know what they need. Which question might reveal what would help?
Offer a specific practical favour or ask whether someone wants company?
The support people appreciate can change according to the situation, not only their personality.
Giving useful support includes respecting when someone prefers to handle a problem alone.
Which type of help do you find hardest to ask for, and why?
Recall someone helping you without making you feel obligated to return the favour.
Two friends want to support the same person but have conflicting ideas. How should they coordinate?
Receive support quietly without discussion or talk through the situation with someone you trust?
What makes certain everyday rituals feel meaningful between people?
Tell me about a small routine that strengthened a friendship without anybody planning it.
Two people stop sharing a routine because their schedules change. How might they preserve what mattered about it?
Share a meal once a month or exchange a short update at the end of each week?
A ritual becomes important when people attach meaning to the time spent together.
Revisiting a shared routine occasionally keeps it from becoming an obligation.
Which repeated activity has helped you understand somebody better over time?
Describe a simple tradition whose meaning changed as you grew older.
Your family wants to include a distant relative in a yearly custom. What parts of the custom could travel?
Keep a familiar tradition going or create one that fits your present circumstances better?
How does your understanding of a person change when you meet their closest friends?
Recall learning an unexpected side of someone's personality through the people they care about.
Two people have strong friendships in different circles. How could they introduce their friends without forcing closeness?
Learn about somebody through their favourite memories or through the people who inspire them?
A person's social circles often reflect different stages and parts of their life.
Having separate friendships is compatible with building a close relationship.
What do you hope the people close to you understand about how you choose friends?
Tell me about a person who connected different parts of your life unexpectedly.
Someone in a new relationship feels pressured to abandon an old friendship. What questions should they explore?
Spend time with friends who challenge your ideas or those who share your long-standing interests?
